title: Lojong Teaching 3
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The main teaching of tonight's Soto Zen dharma talk emphasizes the importance of cultivating a mindful and humble approach to life, letting go of ego-driven motivations and conditioning. By practicing mindfulness, developing bodhicitta, and focusing on benefiting all beings without exception, individuals can overcome their habitual patterns and find space in their lives. This involves acknowledging our limitations, taking responsibility for our actions, and interacting with the world in a more open and compassionate way.

sentences.text: Good evening, everybody.
Thank you for being here.
On Saturday morning we got to welcome back Marv Waschke, who's been away after heart surgery for some months.
Tonight we got to welcome back Jeff McKenna, who's been away after a back injury for some months, a couple of months on the couch pretty much, sounds like.

Tonight I thought we'd have the third of three talks reviewing and considering the Lojong mind training points from Indo-Tibetan Buddhism, which our guiding teacher Norman Fischer brought up at sesshin a couple of months ago.

I've been experimenting a little bit with styles of talk, and so I'm going to experiment again and have tonight's talk be a little more like a class, and not so much me just giving a talk with discussion afterwards.
We'll have some discussion points during the talk.
For the talk you'll have a partner, so we'll have time to break into discussion briefly, for a minute or two, with a partner and then just return.
Rather than rearranging the room several times, we can just turn in place.
So let's find out who your partner is, so we don't have to worry that one has from kindergarten.
We can just go in pairs.
Maybe there's an even number of people, so it would be you two guys, and two and two.
John, I'm going to scoot over a little bit towards Kathy, and then Dale and I don't remember your name, two and two, yeah, that works out, and then Latona and Fran.
So do you know your partner?
I want you to take a moment and introduce yourself.
You know each other, right?
And then, being a little class, we should have a handout in front of us, I think.
I hope we have enough.
John, would you look on the table?
There are some handouts I made a while ago, and hopefully there's still enough.
It's a list of all these slogans.
You can start those around.
Does it seem like there's twenty of those left?
Okay.

So, these Lojong mind training slogans: one thing about them is that it's a little overwhelming, because there's a lot of them, 59 of them, and many of them are written in a little bit of a cryptic way, like you have to know what it actually means.
What we did in the previous two talks was that I didn't talk about all of them, but we talked about a few highlights in the first five points.
It's 59 slogans organized into seven points, like groups.

I want to just mention very briefly the ones we already talked about, and then tonight talk about several slogans from the last two points, point six and point seven, which have quite a few more slogans in them.
Luckily, some of them are pretty simple, and so we'll just see how that goes.
All right, so be ready at a moment's notice to talk to your partner.
We'll get into talking mode and then we'll go back to listening and being in a whole group.
Also feel free to stop me with questions if I say something that doesn't make any sense, or you think of something important.
Sure, can someone give us more light?
Thank you, thank you, Edie. [unclear: "He's"] kind of small type on this handout, didn't I?
People might have their reading glasses.
Yeah, these days it's like everything depends on one's reading glasses.

All right, so before we get into the nitty-gritty, I want to read to you a few pages from Pema Chodron, who's a principal student of Trungpa Rinpoche, who himself is a principal introducer of these teachings to the West.
Pema Chodron actually talks about how she's practiced with these slogans, which I think is the most interesting.
She wrote the foreword, and she did a good job, a really short foreword, so let's read her foreword.
She said:

*I am both honored and delighted to have been asked to write this preface to the new edition of [unclear: "Chodron"] Trungpa Rinpoche's marvelous book about training the mind in the ways of loving kindness and compassion.
Since 1981 the 59 slogans that are contained in this book have been my primary focus of personal practice and of my teaching.*
So this is what she works on, these slogans.
*For all these years I have contemplated Trungpa Rinpoche's commentaries on the slogans almost daily and I can say without exaggeration that they have transformed my life.
The method I have used in this continually deepening exploration is one that Trungpa Rinpoche recommended to his students.

Using a set of cards printed with each of these slogans I shuffle the stack each morning and draw one slogan for the day and then I read from this book about what Trungpa Rinpoche had to say about the slogan.
Sometimes jotting notes on the back of the card*
which is helpful, because some of them are a little cryptic, you know.
*And this is followed by my best try to live by the meaning of that slogan throughout my day.
Sometimes I forget the slogan all day long only to be reminded of its message when I come back to my room at night.
Usually however if something challenging arises the slogan of the day or perhaps a different one all together comes to mind and provides me with some on-the-spot instruction.
This always introduces me to a bigger perspective.*
That's an interesting point: this always introduces me to a bigger perspective.
*I begin to have increased confidence that I can utilize these slogans and be less reactive and see things more clearly throughout my whole life.
Slogan practice indeed continues to help me transform all circumstances into the path of enlightenment.
Even the most difficult of situations has become more and more workable.
The more I get hooked by what is going on the more these challenges become remarkable teacher and a teacher that can open and soften me and make me wiser.*
So that's interesting.
She's saying, I haven't gotten good at floating through life like a cloud and not noticing what's happening.
I've actually gotten more hooked by life, you know what I mean?
Life sucks me in more than it used to, but it's good because then there's teaching there and I can work with it.

*The key however is to acknowledge that I am hooked and to work with the slogan rather than to continue to get all worked up because we are all already experts at escalating our emotional reactivity.*
Isn't that true?
We're experts at that.
*Fanning the fire with habitual thoughts and predictable strategies.
For me the slogan contemplation interrupts this momentum and brings a fresh take into the dynamic.
My gratitude to this practice and to my teacher [unclear: "Troyon Rompachet"]*
*is limitless.
I feel there's no way I could sufficiently repay his kindness into introducing me to these profound yet simple teachings and encouraging me to practice them.
As [unclear: "Rompachet"] says in the introduction of this book, you can just follow the book and do as it says, which is extraordinarily powerful and such a relief.
These words certainly resonate with my personal experience and I am eager that others also give this practice a try.
I feel sure that by taking these words to heart many will profit as I have.
May you be one of those fortunate ones now and in the future.*
So very enthusiastic from [unclear: "Chodron Rompachet"], and they sell this.
You can buy this deck from Shambhala International.
You can buy the deck of cards.
I don't think we need to learn all 59 slogans, but I think it's really interesting to study them and see what are the three or four or five that are ours.
What are our slogans?
They may be ones I mentioned tonight or they may be other ones.
So now to work, quickly reviewing the first five points.
The first point was to train in the preliminaries, to actually create space in our lives for spaciousness itself.
To have a regular practice of some kind.
A regular way that we take five and notice what we're actually feeling and doing.
Maybe that's meditation practice in the morning.
Maybe it's remembering to stop and pause after a meal or when crossing a doorway or whatever it is.
Picking up the telephone.
So, to train in the preliminaries.
Would you please turn to your partner and, just for a moment, have a conversation about this.
How are you doing with training in the preliminaries?
Is this something that feels steady, or that comes and goes, or it doesn't make sense, or that is boring, or is interesting?
And I think with these little conversations, we won't ring bells or have any particular structure.
Just speak with each other and give each other some space.
Listen to what each other has to say.
How is it for you with training in the preliminaries?
What is that for you, and what interests you in that area?
Okay, please.
Just for a minute.
Please just finish that thought, and when you're ready, turn towards the middle.
This is kind of fun.
Now what's great is you don't have to worry if you're cut off, because in a few minutes we'll just go back into it.
And it's all the same topic really.
It's just our life.
So then we talked about what's listed on the sheet here.
The second point is listed as formal practice, and Trungpa Rinpoche emphasizes that the point of that is the development of bodhicitta.
We talked about bodhicitta, the mind of awakening.
The mind that, instead of moving towards what do I get and what do I want and what am I trying to avoid, instead moves out and opens up.
The mind that naturally seeks kindness and awakening for everybody.
So Trungpa Rinpoche emphasizes that the points in the second point are all about developing this bodhicitta.
And the ones that I talked about are the first one, regarding all dharmas as dreams.
That's the way we get caught on this gritty apparent permanence and immovability of reality.
We think it's really real in a way that it isn't.
And so this one is to see things in a more dreamlike way.
Not to deny the reality but to look at the reality differently.
And we talked about the fifth one down there: sending and taking should be practiced alternately.
These two should ride the breath.
This is the description of a Tibetan meditation process called Tonglen, which means sending and receiving.
We talked a lot about the bodhisattva's willingness to absorb trouble.
To take in poison.
To be more interested in relieving the suffering of others than in being right or getting what we want.
And so this Tonglen practice is about that.
It's about mentally, or even literally, absorbing trouble.
Sucking in trouble and breathing out ease and joy.
So we talked about that.
And I think we just glanced at all the other ones, but there's a lot there, more than we have time for.
So this is the practices of developing bodhicitta.
I talked a little bit about point three, and then we'll return to our pairs because they're together.
What inspires us to develop bodhicitta in this system of training?
What really inspires us and helps us is adversity.
You would think nurturing and love and lots of wonderful support would be what inspires us.
That is part of it for sure.
But these teachings understand trouble and difficulty, like Pema Chodron was talking about in her introduction, as teachers and as support for practice that wake us up and help us practice.
And so the very first point basically says exactly that.
We didn't talk about it, but it's obvious it says that.
It says:
*When the world is filled with evil, transform all mishaps into the path of bodhi.*
Bodhi means awakening.
But we talked a lot, in two different talks, about the next one, which is a big one for us it seems, because we have various reactions to this, which is: drive all blames into one.
We read [unclear: "Trump and Rupert Shuk's"] commentary, and he talks about this very literally.
He says when you're in a conflict with anybody, take the blame.
All of it.
Don't worry about who's right, who's wrong.
Just say, "I'm really sorry, it's all my fault."
And really feel that.
Some of us were a little reactive to that.
It didn't sound right.
And we had various justifications for why it wouldn't be good to do that.
It probably just caused confusion and might prevent people from learning from their mistakes, and all this.
And so then we read Pema Chodron, who was a little softer, and she said, well, think about the incredible power of blame.
Think about the way blame has basically unhinged the entire world and Really study that, and study how do you relate to blame.
Do you blame yourself?
Do you blame others?
Really take up blame as a practice point.
She was a little more flexible, but you don't have to always take all the blame, I guess.
So that was interesting, and I'm curious to have you talk to each other about blame.
What is blame for you?
And then along with taking the blame is to be grateful to everyone, the next one.
In one of the discussions I was in, somebody said, "Well, how about there are people who stole from me?
I'm not grateful about that.
What is this?"
Being grateful to everyone, in the context of a difficult situation where there's blame, means the bodhisattva in this system is grateful to be able to take the blame.
You know what I mean?
"Oh, thank you.
I now have the opportunity to take the blame and to practice humility and let go of my point of view and just set my sort of burden of meanness down and just take the blame.
I'm grateful for that."
So we talked about that, and then we talked about the last one, which all works together beautifully: whatever you meet unexpectedly, join with meditation, which I think is a wonderful training.
And there's a later one about the unexpected in a later point.
Basically it's wonderful to come to the Dharma Hall, where you know what to expect and we're very protective of the schedule.
We make a little teeny change, we're very cautious and have discussions.
It's not too much unexpected here, right?
What's inside the mind can be a little unexpected maybe, but basically it's pretty good, pretty steady, and it's very supportive.
We can practice meditation here and develop that and develop our hearts.
But where meditation is really useful and important is: what about the seventeen thousand other times today when something really unexpected happened?
And likely it was something unexpected that you did not like.
It was not what you wanted.
The phone rang and somebody was talking to you in a way that you didn't appreciate.
Then how do you practice?
Then can you bring up your meditation practice in that context?

Okay, so let's turn back to our partners and talk about whatever is up for us about these two points: the practices that bring up bodhicitta and use adversity to do that, especially blame and gratitude and the unexpected.
Good?
Okay, please continue your conversations.
Nice to have a passionate interaction like that and then to return to silence together.
It makes one wish that there was more support in our culture for that, you know.
And all the big meaning at work.
Let's be quiet for about five minutes.
So let's continue our work here.
Those were the first three points.
I think I'm going to skip the fourth point.
It's sort of in code.
There's all these other teachings that go along with the five strengths, and then there's a lot of stuff.
Tibetan Buddhism is quite famous for a careful and meticulous study of death, and so these are practices essentially to prepare for death, which is what life is, right.
So let's skip life and death for now.
We've got other things to talk about.
But the main source for these talks, and also Norman's talks, is this book of talks that I read the introduction to, called Training the Mind.
The chapter in there is really good on this one.
You can read it.
It's a whole series of talks in itself, really.

And so let's talk about the fifth point, which is called here on the handout "yardsticks," which seems to suggest or imply some way of measuring our progress, which we have to admit we have a strong interest in.
How are we doing?
I talked about two of the four points last time.
The second one is interesting because it seems in a way to contradict many of the other points about bodhicitta.
There's a strong emphasis in these teachers on putting others first, treasuring others, taking the blame for others, taking poison away from others.
And then the second point here is a sort of balance to that: of the two witnesses, hold the principal one.
The two witnesses are yourself and everybody else, and the principal one is yourself.
So this point is saying really trust yourself.
Deeply feel what you feel you really need to be doing in your life, and really trust that.
Or, another way to look at it, don't live your life so the others will like you, or so it will look good.
Last talk I remembered a really wonderful teaching that I heard once from one of my teachers in San Francisco, Blanche Hartman.
I'll tell this whole story again because it's such a good story.
She was recounting when she was first at San Francisco Zen Center, which was a very vibrant and intense Zen Center early in American Zen.
They were very gung ho, you know what I mean.
Many people were living at the center and everyone was practicing full time, and they were all in their early twenties and some even teenagers, actually.
John Bales was there as a teenager.
Blanche Hartman was in her early forties, so she felt always a little out of it, and she was never cool enough, and therefore she had to try harder.
She was always trying to be really good at it and learn as much as she could.

One time somehow Baker Roshi, who was one of the teachers there for a while, cottoned on to this, and he said to her in dokusan or something, "For the rest of the day today, don't do anything for the sake of somebody else.
Don't do anything for the sake of somebody else."
And she said, "Oh sure, no big deal."
But as soon as she left the room, she found that every single thing she was doing was for somebody else: to impress somebody, to help somebody, to get some support from somebody you know.
It was all to do with looking out to everybody else and nothing much to do with the principal witness, with what her heart really needed.
So that's interesting.
These things are all double-edged swords, right?
If you worry too much about others, you're confused.
You worry too much about yourself, you're confused anyway.
But there's that one.
And then the other one we talked about, which goes along with the last point of point three, the last point on this one: if you can practice even when distracted, you are well trained.
It's one thing to gather oneself and be in touch with the breath and realize there's something difficult coming up and work with that as best you can, which is beautiful and important.
We should all do that.
But it's another thing when something just comes out of left field.
You're not ready, you're distracted, you're too busy, you're already a little tired, you're grumpy, you're at home with your family, and you don't want to deal with this right now.
Why is it my wife brings up the toughest issues about 11 o'clock at night?
It's to train me, it's to help me train on this point.
So I am always grateful for that.
I don't know why these are yardsticks exactly, but it's just more points: trusting your own heart, and appreciating when you're distracted, because that's a real opportunity for practice.
So, new material at last, you've been wondering.
These have many points, and some of them are pretty simple.
Many of the slogans, excuse me, the sixth point is called commitments in some places, in other places it's called disciplines.
I want to touch on five or six of these.
I want to talk about the second one: change your attitude but remain natural.
Pretty interesting.
In other words, really work on yourself, really be willing to change, really transform how you live your life, but still be in touch with the naturalness of living.
We know people who... and I think one's growth and development has a sort of cycle, where at some point in the cycle you're trying too hard and you're pretty artificial, right?
Your friends don't want to be around you for a while, and then you settle back into something more natural.
So I think there's a cycle that's implied here.
Change your attitude but remain natural: don't force it.
The next one, the third one there, is don't talk about injured limbs.
Injured limbs means other people's quirks, other people's problems, other people's annoying little habits or whatever, which from your point of view seem like an injury.
It says don't talk about that.
It may not be helpful to talk about that.
Just work with people as they are.

We talk about this a lot in precept study, right, in Zen: when we talk too much about people's limitations and hang-ups, there's a way that we make those hang-ups more rigid, more solid and more real, and sort of collude in making sure the person always acts that way.
She's a little unreliable, so I'm not going to give her any responsibilities, and then I help her be unreliable in any way I can.
So, don't talk about injured limbs.
The next one's about the same, but the one after that is interesting: work with the greatest defilements first.
What are your biggest hang-ups, your biggest problems?
Don't put that off.
This goes with all the teachings on the immediacy of the moment.
Why do we think there's a later when we're going to get to deal with these problems?
For now I'll just kind of deal with this stuff, but then later on...
So, work with the greatest defilements first.
Right after that, as if pairing with it: abandon any hope of fruition.
This is encouragement, and it's like in Zen where we say have no gaining idea.
It's the same idea: have no gaining idea.
It does not mean that there isn't gain and there isn't fruition.
It means abandon your hope of fruition.
It's not a denial of fruition, it's a release from clinging to result, clinging to getting something later.
So, abandoning that hope.
The next one is abandoning poisonous food.
Poisonous food is a metaphor, as you might imagine, and the primary point of this one seems to be: don't make Dharma practice itself into a sort of ego-boosting poison.
It's a point about spiritual pride.
The first point about it is spiritual pride, but the second point is literally abandoning poisonous inputs, poisonous food.
Most of us are pretty careful about what we eat.
We've all reduced, most of us, the back of Bob's truck probably doesn't suggest this, but let's just have a boy and reduced our junk food, sorry.
Most of us are trying to be mindful about what we put into our mouth.
But what about what we put into our eyes, what we put into our ears?
What do we watch, what are we listening to, what are we reading, what are we thinking about?
Can we reduce the poison and distraction that enters into our life that way?
So, banning poisonous food, and I Want to get the next two.
This was really interesting, in relationships: don't wait in ambush.
Don't wait in ambush.
Once I read that, I thought, gosh, that's something we do.
In other words, it means don't sort of wait and collude and look for the opportunity to say "I told you so," essentially.
We sort of think so-and-so is going to be this way, so-and-so is going to do this to me, so I'm just going to wait until she does that, so I can say, "Look, you're always doing that."
I think in an intimate relationship there's a way that we wait in ambush.
We have our little things that we know trigger us, and we let them build up, and we're sort of ready to ambush the person.
And then to the other side, one more, and then we'll go back to our discussions.
There are quite a few different things here, but I want to just talk about the middle one there: don't act with a twist.
Don't act with a twist.
And that's really only [unclear: "read you trunk comments"] and don't act with a twist.
Acting with a twist means that since you think you're going to get the best in any case, you might as well volunteer for the worst.
This is very sneaky.
You could act with a twist in dealing with your teacher, your students, your life situation, everything.
You could pretend to be a completely benevolent person who always takes the blame, realizing all along that you're going to get the best.
It's pretty straightforward, I think.
Acting with a twist is a form of spiritual materialism.
It's having an ulterior motive.
I think that's the essential nature of having a twist: you have this ulterior motive that you're masking, of working actually for your own benefit.

For instance, in order to gain good results for yourself, you may temporarily take the blame for everything, or you may practice Lojong really hard in order to get something from it, or with the idea of protecting yourself from something.
So the practice of the slogan is to drop that attitude of looking for personal benefit from practice, either as an immediate or as a long-term result.
In other words, a way of acting with a twist in our practice is: well, I'll practice humility and I'll renounce any gain, because I know that's how I'm going to get lots of gain.
I know that's probably going to work, because they said don't have any gain, so I'm not... okay, so that's that kind of thing.
It's sort of fun to make jokes of these things, but it requires some real study.
It requires really bringing these things up and seeing, because there's a certain level of unawareness that we have to acknowledge and touch in our practice and in our lives.
Some things we're aware of, some things we're not so aware of.

That's the point of these kinds of slogans, or of saying the precepts, which we do in a similar way: to have this little tool, this little magnifying glass, as we go through our day, and say, "Well, I wonder if I'm acting with a twist right now.
Well, I don't think so.
Well, wait a minute, just a second here.
I think I have this sort of ulterior motive.
I'm pretending to be kind of nice to my co-worker, but really I'm hoping that she is completely shamed in this meeting, and I will benefit."
Or who knows what it is.
It can be very subtle.

The other thing I think is interesting to look at, and I think the way Trungpa writes about this is not so helpful in a way, is that he always seems to be strongly trying to encourage his students to be less self-centered.
So in his comments he's always sort of pushing them to consider others, do this for others.
But we are not different from others, that's the thing.
So are there ways that we're acting with a twist towards ourselves, like harming ourselves with sort of sneakiness about our own heart and our own needs?

So, a whole bunch of things: changing your attitude but remaining neutral, not talking about injured limbs, working with our defilements, abandoning the clinging to results, reducing our poisonous food, not waiting in ambush, and not acting with a twist.
What's left [unclear: "on her"]?
Shall we talk for a minute?
Let's see, what are these things for you?
What's up for you in your life about these things?
Are you hearing?
I think you're hearing.
Yes.

**Participant:** One of the things I was really appreciating earlier, coming into the zendo, and this evening while we were practicing, is that sense of the limitless potential of stillness, you know what I mean?
You quiet down a little bit, and you notice there's a lot more stillness available even below that.
And you settle down a little more, and there's more below that.
And I suppose it depends on one's conditioning.
One could be maybe frustrated by that, like, ah, I'm not very good, obviously.
But it feels very nurturing to me at the moment.
There's always more stillness, more peace.
**Nomon Tim Burnett:** So, guidelines for practicing mind training, point seven.
First one, first slogan: all activities should be done with one intention.
One intention.
And the one intention, as you might have guessed, is the intention to benefit.
Trungpa Rinpoche writes "to benefit others," but it may be better for us to say to benefit all beings, including, you know, we're included.
But we're no more privileged than any other being.
We're just another manifestation of life in the situation.
This would be a great slogan for us, I think, going through the day: to just look and see, is this activity being done with the intention to benefit all beings?
And then [unclear: "skipping one to two activities"].
One at the beginning, one at the end.
And this is a very concrete suggestion.

It's just like what Pema Chodron was talking about: to practice, at the beginning of the day, bringing up our intention, whether it's through one of these slogans or through another practice we're doing, to bring up our intention in being a practitioner for the day.
And I've been chanting a little verse to myself in the morning, which I've really enjoyed.
But then what I don't often do is the other half.
And then one at the end.
So at the end of the day, look back over the day: how'd it go today?
And I think this is a trick for us.
Can we do that in a way that doesn't just beat ourselves up, like another failed day of practice?
To just notice, okay, here's my day, I brought up my intention.
Sometimes I carried it forth, sometimes I forgot.
This is my human life.
Tomorrow, I'll start all over again.
So two activities, one at the beginning, one at the end.
And the next one is great for us.
Whichever of the two occurs, be patient.
And the two are, in this case, when good things happen, be patient.
When bad things happen, be patient.
So it's a real instruction on equanimity, right?
On steadiness.
One thing that's absolutely reliable is change and impermanence.
When conditions which we think of as good arise, they are gonna go.
When conditions we feel are bad arise, they will also go.
And we can just be steady in the middle of that.
So whichever of the two occurs, be patient.
And skipping one to train in the three difficulties.
This last set has lots of numbered lists, and they don't list them in the slogan, so you just have to know.
So train in the three difficulties.
So the three difficulties here are, number one, the difficulty of noticing when you're being fooled by your conditioning.
Number one is the difficulty in noticing: oh, I just got tripped up by my reactivity, by my habit, by my usual mode, whatever.
And the second difficulty is to actually reduce that, not do that so much.
And the third difficulty is the difficulty of cutting the continuity.
Cutting the continuity.
And so this is where meditation practice really helps.
So the continuity is this sort of tremendous momentum of our personality and our personal story.
This is me zooming through the day, right, with no space, no room to turn around or shift, until you get sick and then you have six weeks on the couch to think about your life.
So cutting the continuity is the ability in the middle of that to say, wait, okay, stop.
And there's multitudes of excellent self-help books and practices and a million things one can do to cut the continuity, but the slogan is to bring up that training, to train in that.
That's my intention: to learn somehow to learn how to notice when I'm being fooled, to reduce how reactive I am and be able to cut that off, to find the space, to find the space in my life.
So that's the three difficulties.
Then there's take on the three principal causes, which is a whole different three, just a different three each time.
The three principal causes are, and they go together though, these causes help us with the difficulties.
The first is to acknowledge that we really do need teachings.
We really do need a teacher and we need teachings.
So in Tibetan yoga, they're very guru centric.

So actually his comment says, we need, his comment is, they recognize you need a teacher, you need a guru, which, maybe you need a guru or mini gurus, but I think more useful to us is you need teachings to sort of acknowledge that there's something bigger than my understanding.
My understanding is limited and I recognize that I need more.
That's the first principal cause.
